summary: Argues that graphics protocols must handle attention, such as a user pointing at something with a light pen, not just describe images to display. Earlier work in RFC 86, RFC 94 and RFC 125 covered the display side. This note addresses interactive input.

plainLanguage.summary: Network graphics need to carry input as well as pictures. This RFC describes kinds of input and proposes a three-part message for telling a graphics program what happened.

questions: what is network graphic attention handling
how should interactive graphics be handled over a network
what types of input devices can graphics systems use
how should network graphics report user input
what information does an attention message carry
subtitle: A proposed structure for reporting input to network graphics applications.

tldr.problem: Earlier network graphics proposals focused on display output, but interactive systems also need to report user and device input.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines attention handling and proposes messages with device identification, data identification and the input data itself.
tldr.outcome: It offers guidelines for a general attention protocol but says detailed bit-level rules remain to be defined.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 178 as Unknown and records no RFC that updates or obsoletes it. The document proposes guidelines and does not define a complete attention protocol.

sections.title: Why Graphics Need Input Handling
sections.content:
Earlier network graphics work described graphic data for display, including the Network Standard Graphic Data Stream proposal. RFC 178 addresses the other direction: how a system receives and handles input such as keystrokes or light-pen use.

Attention handling means detecting a human or device stimulus, interpreting its immediate meaning, and either passing it to a user routine or taking an immediate action. It does not include the detailed application work that the input may request.
sections.plainLanguage: A graphics system must report input, not only send pictures to a screen. Attention handling detects an input and passes its meaning to the right part of the system.

sections.title: Input Devices and Their Data
sections.content:
The RFC surveys pushbuttons and keyboards, analog devices such as shaft encoders and trackballs, tablets, light pens, internal attentions such as programmed traps, and software-generated logical attentions. These devices may produce a key code, a coordinate, a memory address or another value.

An intelligent terminal may process input locally and change its own copy of display data. The host then needs a way to learn about those changes so the display and application do not become inconsistent.
sections.plainLanguage: A keyboard, tablet or light pen can each produce different input data. If a terminal changes a picture locally, it must also tell the host what changed.

sections.title: Three Parts of an Attention Message
sections.content:
The RFC suggests three elements for a terminal-to-host attention message: device identification, data identification and data. Device identification distinguishes the type of input device; identical devices at different network nodes need not be distinguished there.

Data identification describes the following data, including its units, kind and format. The data field carries the input itself and may have arbitrary length and organization. The author presents this as a guideline, not a complete protocol specifying each bit.
sections.plainLanguage: The message says which kind of device produced input, what kind of data follows, and then carries that data. The RFC leaves the exact bit layout for later work.

sections.title: Graphics Across Different Hosts
sections.content:
The RFC describes configurations in which an application, input processor and output processor may be separate or located on different hosts. Standard formats can let an application work with different input and display devices without being designed for each device.

Intelligent terminals may handle some input locally, which makes coordination between the local display and the central application important. The proposed attention message structure is intended to communicate such input in a device-independent way.
sections.plainLanguage: Separating the application from device-specific software can let different screens use the same graphics program. The devices still need a clear way to report their input.
